passages.t: Trust in the LORD with all your heart
passages.happening:
The father asks his son to keep his teaching, ‘for they will add length to your days, years and peace to your life’ (verse 2). ‘Never let loving devotion or faithfulness leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart’ (verse 3).

Then come the book's best-known lines: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight” (verses 5-6). ‘Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil’ (verse 7).

He tells his son to honor the LORD with his wealth and the firstfruits of his harvest, and his barns will be full (verses 9-10).

And he speaks of hard times: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke; for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves from the heart to money, to hardship, and then to the neighbor next door. Wisdom is not a new religion beside Israel's faith. It is that faith lived out in ordinary life.

Binding something around the neck and writing it on a tablet drew on everyday things: ornaments and seals worn at the throat, and the clay or wooden tablets people wrote on. The teaching is to be both visible and inward. It recalls Deuteronomy 6, where God's words are bound on the hand and written on the doorposts.

Loving devotion is chesed, the loyal love that keeps covenant promises, and faithfulness is emet, truth and reliability. These are the words God uses of himself (Exodus 34:6). The son is to wear God's own character like a necklace.

Trust, batach in Hebrew, means to rely on something and feel secure because of it. Its opposite is leaning on your own understanding, a verb for putting your weight on a support. The question is which support will hold.

Firstfruits were the first and best of the crops, brought to God as the law commanded (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:1-11), to say that the land and its harvest belonged to him. The LORD's correction, in verse 12, is the word yakach, to reprove or set right. It is correction that aims at the son's good, the way a father corrects a son he delights in.
passages.later: Moses taught the same about discipline: ‘just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you’ (Deuteronomy 8:5). Hebrews quotes verses 11 and 12 to believers facing hardship, in the Greek wording: “For the Lord disciplines the one He loves” (Hebrews 12:6). It adds, ‘No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it’ (Hebrews 12:11).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter promise long life and full barns to those who trust and honor God?

Verses 2, 9 and 10, and 16 can be read that way, and some teachers have used them to argue that faithfulness guarantees health and wealth. But these are proverbs, observations about how life usually goes under God, not contracts. Wise, generous and honest living does tend toward health and provision, and a community that honors God and treats neighbors justly usually does well.

Yet this same chapter speaks of the LORD's discipline and of hardship in the lives of those he loves (verses 11-12). The rest of Scripture is full of faithful people who were poor, sick, or died young, and Job, Ecclesiastes and many psalms press on exactly those cases. Proverbs shows the normal pattern of God's world and where it is heading. It does not promise that any one faithful life will be free of loss, and reading it as a formula can wound people who are suffering through no fault of their own.

Nor does verse 12 mean that every hardship is a punishment. Hebrews uses it to tell suffering believers that they belong to God, not that their pain is a penalty.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Leaning means putting your weight on something. Ask what you lean on when a decision is hard: your own reading of things, or the LORD. And ask what it would look like to acknowledge him in one ordinary part of your life this week, your money, your work, or a hard season.

passages.t: Better than silver: a tree of life
passages.happening:
Now a hymn in praise of wisdom. ‘Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, the man who acquires understanding’ (verse 13), ‘for she is more profitable than silver, and her gain is better than fine gold’ (verse 14). ‘She is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her’ (verse 15).

‘Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor’ (verse 16). ‘All her ways are pleasant, and all her paths are peaceful’ (verse 17). ‘She is a tree of life to those who embrace her’ (verse 18).

And wisdom was there at the making of the world. ‘The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding’ (verse 19). By his knowledge the deep waters broke open and the clouds dripped with dew (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Rubies and fine gold were the luxury goods of kings and temples. The hymn says that wisdom is worth more than the richest things anyone could own.

The tree of life reaches back to the garden of Eden in Genesis 2 and 3, where it stood in the middle of the garden and was lost when the man and woman were sent out. Proverbs uses the picture several times (11:30; 13:12; 15:4). Wisdom gives back some of what was lost: a life that flourishes.

The last two verses look ahead to chapter 8, where Wisdom will speak of being beside God when he made the world. If God made the world by wisdom, then living wisely means living in step with the way the world was made.
passages.later: The psalms praise the same wise Maker: “How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all” (Psalm 104:24). And the Bible ends where Eden began, with a tree of life by the river of the new Jerusalem: ‘And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations’ (Revelation 22:2).
passages.asks: The hymn sets wisdom above gold and rubies. Ask what you would trade to gain it, and what you have traded it away for. And ask where your own daily paths could be more pleasant and peaceful if they ran with the grain of the world God made.

passages.t: Sweet sleep, and good to the neighbor
passages.happening:
‘My son, do not lose sight of this: Preserve sound judgment and discernment’ (verse 21). Then he will walk safely and not stumble. ‘When you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you rest, your sleep will be sweet’ (verse 24). ‘For the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from the snare’ (verse 26).

Then come five plain commands about neighbors. ‘Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act’ (verse 27). Do not tell a neighbor to come back tomorrow when you have what he needs today (verse 28). Do not plot against a neighbor who lives trustingly beside you (verse 29), or accuse someone without cause (verse 30). ‘Do not envy a violent man or choose any of his ways’ (verse 31).

The chapter closes with contrasts. The LORD ‘is a friend to the upright’ (verse 32). ‘The curse of the LORD is on the house of the wicked, but He blesses the home of the righteous’ (verse 33). ‘He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
These verses assume life in a village where people depended on one another. Telling someone to come back tomorrow, when you could pay or help today, could mean real hardship for a day laborer or a poor family. Israel's law required wages to be paid the same day.

The neighbor who lives ‘trustfully’ beside you is easy to harm precisely because he has no reason to be on guard. Wisdom treats that trust as something to protect, not to use.

The closing contrasts sum up the book's two paths: the perverse and the upright, the wicked and the righteous, the mockers and the humble, fools and the wise. Verse 34 became one of the most quoted lines of the book.
passages.later: The law said of a poor worker: ‘You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them’ (Deuteronomy 24:15). And James and Peter both quote verse 34 in its Greek form: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5).
passages.asks: The commands about neighbors are very concrete. Ask whether there is good you could do today that you have been putting off until tomorrow. And ask whom you are tempted to envy, and what it would mean to choose humility instead, since that is where the verse says grace is given.
